<body>
<div class="mod-frontmatter mod-ui">
<h2 style="text-align: center; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto"><strong style="color: #cc33cc;">The Beginning: Why Machine Learning Exists</strong></h2>
<p dir="auto">Imagine a world where every useful rule can be written by hand:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">A rule for classifying emails<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">A rule for driving a car<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">A rule for detecting diseases<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">A rule for recognizing speech<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Very soon, we realize something powerful:</p>
<blockquote dir="auto">
<p><strong>Most real-world problems are too complex to hand-program.</strong></p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">The boundaries are fuzzy, patterns are hidden, and human intuition is insufficient.</p>
<p dir="auto">Thus the fundamental need arises:</p>
<blockquote dir="auto">
<p><strong>Can a system learn these rules directly from experience?</strong></p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">This is the birth of <strong>machine learning</strong> — the science of building programs that improve by learning from data.</p>
<p dir="auto">But to learn systematically, we must start by defining what a <em>good</em> learning problem is.</p>
<hr>
<hr>
<h2 style="text-align: center; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto"><strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Well-Posed Learning Problems</strong></h2>
<p dir="auto">A learning problem is <em>well-posed</em> when three ingredients are clearly defined:</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto"><strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Component 1 — Task (T)</strong></h3>
<p dir="auto">What must the system learn to do?</p>
<p dir="auto">Examples:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Classify emails as spam or not spam<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Predict house prices<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Recommend movies<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">This is the <strong>goal</strong> of the learner.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Component 2 — Performance Measure (P)</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">How do we know if it is learning?</p>
<p dir="auto">Some common performance measures:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Accuracy<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Error rate<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Mean squared error<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Precision/recall<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">F1 score<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The learning system must know <em>what it is being judged on</em>.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Component 3 — Training Experience (E)</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Where does the learner get information?</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Labeled data<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Unlabeled data<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Rewards or penalties<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Past cases<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Simulated environments<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Experience shapes improvement.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Formal Definition</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">A learning problem is well-posed if:</p>
<blockquote dir="auto">
<p><strong>A system improves at task T, with respect to performance measure P, based on experience E.</strong></p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">This clean, three-part frame is the compass guiding all ML applications.</p>
<hr>
<hr>
<h2 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Designing a Learning System</strong>
</h2>
<p dir="auto">Once we have a well-posed problem, we step into the craft of <strong>designing a learning system</strong>.<br>
This design has four interconnected elements.</p>
<hr>
<h2 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Choosing the Hypothesis Space</strong>
</h2>
<p dir="auto">When we design a learning system, one of the most important decisions — often invisible to beginners — is choosing the <strong>hypothesis space</strong>.</p>
<p dir="auto">The hypothesis space is simply:</p>
<blockquote dir="auto">
<p><strong>The set of all possible models the learner is allowed to consider.</strong></p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">It is the <em>universe</em> of candidate solutions.</p>
<hr>
<h2 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Why This Matters</strong>
</h2>
<p dir="auto">Imagine you are searching for treasure.<br>
If you search only the backyard, you'll never find treasure buried in the mountains.<br>
But if you decide to search the entire earth, you’ll become overwhelmed.</p>
<p dir="auto">Machine learning faces the same dilemma:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Search too <em>narrowly</em> → you miss the true solution.<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Search too <em>widely</em> → you waste time, get confused, or overfit noise.<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Thus the hypothesis space must be <strong>just right</strong> — expressive enough to capture the truth, but constrained enough to avoid nonsense.</p>
<hr>
<h2 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Examples of Hypothesis Spaces</strong>
</h2>
<p dir="auto">Each learning algorithm chooses a different “shape” of functions it can learn.</p>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Linear Models</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">These models assume the world behaves like a line or plane:</p>
<div class="math math-block is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML" display="true"><mjx-math display="true" class="MJX-TEX" style="margin-left: 0px; margin-right: 0px;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c210E TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c3D"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-msub space="4"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D464 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: -0.15em;"><mjx-mn class="mjx-n" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c30"></mjx-c></mjx-mn></mjx-script></mjx-msub><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="3"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2B"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-msub space="3"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D464 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: -0.15em;"><mjx-mn class="mjx-n" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c31"></mjx-c></mjx-mn></mjx-script></mjx-msub><mjx-msub><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: -0.15em;"><mjx-mn class="mjx-n" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c31"></mjx-c></mjx-mn></mjx-script></mjx-msub><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="3"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2B"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="3"><mjx-c class="mjx-c22EF"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="3"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2B"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-msub space="3"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D464 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: -0.15em;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D45B TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi></mjx-script></mjx-msub><mjx-msub><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: -0.15em;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D45B TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi></mjx-script></mjx-msub></mjx-math></mjx-container></div>
<p dir="auto">Pros:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Fast<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Easy to interpret<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Good when relationships are roughly straight-line<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Cons:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Cannot model curves or complex interactions<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Too simple for many real-world tasks<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Linear models live in a <strong>small hypothesis space</strong>.</p>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Decision Trees</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Decision trees break the space using yes/no rules:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">“Is age &gt; 30?”<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">“Is income &lt; ₹50k?”<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">“Is color = red?”<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Each path through the tree is a simple decision-making route.</p>
<p dir="auto">Pros:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Interpretability<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Works with categorical features<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Cons:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Can grow too complex<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Highly sensitive to noise<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Hypothesis space can be <strong>very large</strong> if trees grow deep.</p>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Neural Networks</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Neural networks allow layers of computation:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Hidden neurons<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Activation functions<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Deep hierarchies<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">They can represent an enormous variety of functions, including extremely complex ones.</p>
<p dir="auto">Pros:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Can approximate <em>any</em> function<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Good at learning patterns from images, sound, text<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Cons:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Easy to overfit<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Requires large data<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">This is a <strong>massive hypothesis space</strong> — almost too powerful if not controlled.</p>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Support Vector Machines</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">SVMs find separating boundaries — hyperplanes — in higher-dimensional spaces.<br>
With kernels, they can learn curves, circles, spirals, and more.</p>
<p dir="auto">Pros:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Very powerful with kernels<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Elegant mathematical foundation<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Cons:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Harder to interpret<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Kernel choice matters<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Hypothesis space depends on the kernel:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Linear kernel → limited<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">RBF kernel → extremely flexible<br>
</li>
</ul>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Probabilistic Models</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">These models assume the data was generated by a probability process:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Naive Bayes<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Gaussian mixtures<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Hidden Markov models<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">They search among functions that <strong>represent distributions</strong>.</p>
<p dir="auto">Pros:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Uncertainty built-in<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Natural interpretation<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Cons:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Assumptions may be violated<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Can be too rigid or too loose<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Hypothesis space depends on model assumptions.</p>
<hr>
<h2 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">The Balance: Underfitting vs. Overfitting</strong>
</h2>
<p dir="auto">Selecting a hypothesis space is a balancing act.</p>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Too Simple → Underfitting</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">The model cannot capture the true relationship.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Linear model trying to fit a sine wave<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Shallow decision tree for a complex dataset<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Low-degree polynomial for highly curved data<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Symptoms:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">High bias<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Poor performance even on training data<br>
</li>
</ul>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Too Complex → Overfitting</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">The model captures patterns that aren’t real — it memorizes noise.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Deep trees<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Too many neural network layers<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Very flexible kernels<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">High-degree polynomials<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Symptoms:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Very low training error<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Very poor test error<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Model becomes unstable<br>
</li>
</ul>
<hr>
<h2 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">How ML Designers Think About Hypothesis Space</strong>
</h2>
<p dir="auto">Choosing the hypothesis space is guided by:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Domain knowledge</strong><br>
(“Stock prices rarely follow straight lines — use a flexible model.”)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Data quantity</strong><br>
(Small datasets demand simpler hypothesis spaces.)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Risk of overfitting</strong><br>
(More complexity → more danger.)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Computational cost</strong><br>
(Large hypothesis spaces require more processing.)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Interpretability needs</strong><br>
(Doctors need explainable models; finance may require transparency.)<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">This choice often determines whether learning is possible at all.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">A Simple Illustration (Mini Example)</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Suppose you want to model temperature throughout the day.</p>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Option A: Linear Model (Too simple)</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">A line cannot capture morning rise, noon peak, evening drop.</p>
<p dir="auto">Underfits badly.</p>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Option B: 10th-degree Polynomial (Too complex)</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">It wiggles through every point, capturing noise (wind gusts, random fluctuations).</p>
<p dir="auto">Overfits disastrously.</p>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Option C: Smooth curve (like a sinusoidal function)</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Captures essential shape — morning rise, gradual fall — without insanity.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>This is the ideal hypothesis space.</strong></p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Summary</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Choosing the hypothesis space is one of the most critical design decisions in machine learning.</p>
<p dir="auto">It defines:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">What the learner <em>can</em> learn<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">What patterns are considered plausible<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">How vulnerable the model is to noise<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">How generalizable the final solution will be<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">A good hypothesis space is not the biggest or the smallest —<br>
it is the one that reflects a realistic, balanced understanding of the problem.</p>
<hr>
<hr>
<h2 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Choosing the Target Function (Unknown)</strong>
</h2>
<p dir="auto">When we study machine learning, we often talk about <em>learning a function</em> — as if there is some hidden mathematical rule out there, waiting for us to uncover it.</p>
<p dir="auto">But what exactly is this “rule”?<br>
Why do we call it a <em>target function</em>?<br>
And why do we say it is <em>unknown</em>?</p>
<p dir="auto">To understand this, we need to look at the world from the perspective of a machine learning algorithm.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">The World Always Has a Hidden Mechanism</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Every real-world phenomenon has some mechanism behind it.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Whether an email is spam or not<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Whether a patient has a disease<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Whether a customer will buy a product<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">What is the price of a house<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Whether the weather will be sunny<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">In theory, there is always a <strong>true underlying process</strong> that determines the output from the input — even if that process is messy, probabilistic, or partly random.</p>
<p dir="auto">We call this hidden process the <strong>target function</strong>, denoted:</p>
<div class="math math-block is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML" display="true"><mjx-math display="true" class="MJX-TEX" style="margin-left: 0px; margin-right: 0px;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D453 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-math></mjx-container></div>
<p dir="auto">It is the true mapping from inputs to outputs.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">In spam detection:<br>
(f(x)) decides if this email <em>is truly</em> spam<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">In disease diagnosis:<br>
(f(x)) determines if the patient <em>actually has</em> the disease<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">In regression:<br>
(f(x)) produces the real-world numeric value<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">This function exists, whether or not we understand it.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">The Target Function Is Hidden From Us</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">We never get to see this target function directly.</p>
<p dir="auto">For example:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">We don’t see the exact biological equation mapping symptoms → disease<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">We don’t know the true rule mapping pixels → “cat” or “dog”<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">We don’t know the true psychological reason behind buying behavior<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">We don’t know the exact financial mechanism behind house pricing<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">What we observe is only a <strong>limited set of examples</strong>, like shadows on a wall.</p>
<p dir="auto">We see:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Inputs (x)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Outputs (y)<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">But never the underlying rule (f(x)).</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Machine Learning Is the Art of Approximating f(x)</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Since the true function is hidden (unknown), we attempt to build an <strong>approximation</strong>, called the hypothesis:</p>
<div class="math math-block is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML" display="true"><mjx-math display="true" class="MJX-TEX" style="margin-left: 0px; margin-right: 0px;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c210E TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-math></mjx-container></div>
<p dir="auto">This hypothesis is the model’s guess of what (f(x)) might be.</p>
<p dir="auto">The goal is:</p>
<div class="math math-block is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML" display="true"><mjx-math display="true" class="MJX-TEX" style="margin-left: 0px; margin-right: 0px;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c210E TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2248"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D453 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-math></mjx-container></div>
<p dir="auto">But we will never expect <strong>perfect equality</strong> because:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">The training data is finite<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">The world is noisy<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Labels may be imperfect<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">True relationships may be extremely complex<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Real processes may depend on hidden variables not present in the data<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Thus, we aim for <strong>best approximation</strong>, not perfection.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Why We Need to Choose a Target Function Form</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Although the true (f(x)) is unknown, we must <em>choose</em> what kind of relationship we believe exists.</p>
<p dir="auto">This is not guessing blindly; it’s guided by domain knowledge.</p>
<p dir="auto">Examples:</p>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Linear regression assumption</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">We assume:</p>
<div class="math math-block is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML" display="true"><mjx-math display="true" class="MJX-TEX" style="margin-left: 0px; margin-right: 0px;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D453 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2248"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-msup space="4"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D464 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: 0.413em;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D447 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi></mjx-script></mjx-msup><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="3"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2B"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" space="3"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D44F TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi></mjx-math></mjx-container></div>
<p dir="auto">This means we believe:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">The underlying pattern is mostly linear<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Noise exists, but trend is straight<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Inputs combine additively<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">For some problems, this is very reasonable.</p>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Neural network assumption</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">We assume:</p>
<div class="math math-block is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML" display="true"><mjx-math display="true" class="MJX-TEX" style="margin-left: 0px; margin-right: 0px;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D453 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2248"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c210E TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c3D"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D70E TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-msub><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D44A TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: -0.15em; margin-left: -0.104em;"><mjx-mn class="mjx-n" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c32"></mjx-c></mjx-mn></mjx-script></mjx-msub><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2C"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" space="2"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D70E TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-msub><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D44A TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: -0.15em; margin-left: -0.104em;"><mjx-mn class="mjx-n" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c31"></mjx-c></mjx-mn></mjx-script></mjx-msub><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-math></mjx-container></div>
<p dir="auto">That is:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">The target function can be nonlinear<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">It may have hierarchical structure<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Complex interactions exist<br>
</li>
</ul>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Decision tree assumption</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">We assume:</p>
<div class="math math-block is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML" display="true"><mjx-math display="true" class="MJX-TEX" style="margin-left: 0px; margin-right: 0px;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D453 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mtext class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-cA0"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c63"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c61"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c6E"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c20"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c62"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c65"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c20"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c65"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c78"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c70"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c72"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c65"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c73"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c73"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c65"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c64"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c20"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c61"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c73"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c20"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c61"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c20"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c73"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c65"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c71"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c75"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c65"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c6E"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c63"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c65"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c20"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c6F"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c66"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c20"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c69"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c66"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c2013"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c74"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c68"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c65"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c6E"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c20"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c72"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c75"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c6C"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c65"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c73"></mjx-c></mjx-mtext></mjx-math></mjx-container></div>
<p dir="auto">This means:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">The world can be split using yes/no questions<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Some features have threshold behavior<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Interpretability is important<br>
</li>
</ul>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">kNN assumption</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">We assume:</p>
<div class="math math-block is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML" display="true"><mjx-math display="true" class="MJX-TEX" style="margin-left: 0px; margin-right: 0px;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D453 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2248"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D453 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-msup><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: 0.413em;"><mjx-mo class="mjx-var" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2032"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-script></mjx-msup><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mstyle><mjx-mspace style="width: 1em;"></mjx-mspace></mjx-mstyle><mjx-mtext class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c69"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c66"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-cA0"></mjx-c></mjx-mtext><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mtext class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-cA0"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c69"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c73"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c20"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c63"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c6C"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c6F"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c73"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c65"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c20"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c74"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c6F"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-cA0"></mjx-c></mjx-mtext><mjx-msup><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: 0.413em;"><mjx-mo class="mjx-var" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2032"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-script></mjx-msup></mjx-math></mjx-container></div>
<p dir="auto">This is a very human view of learning:</p>
<blockquote dir="auto">
<p>“Similar cases have similar outcomes.”</p>
</blockquote>
<hr>
<p dir="auto">In each case, we are making an educated <strong>assumption</strong> about the shape of the target function.</p>
<p dir="auto">This assumption defines what kind of hypothesis the model can produce.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">The Learner Does Not Choose f(x); It Chooses h(x)</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Since we cannot see the true function (f(x)), the model is forced to:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Choose a hypothesis space (linear? tree? neural network?)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Search within that space<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Find the best hypothesis (h(x)) based on training examples<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">This gives a new perspective:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>The target function exists independently of our model.</strong><br>
</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>The hypothesis is our best attempt to approximate it.</strong><br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The quality of learning depends on:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">How expressive our hypothesis space is<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">How well our algorithm searches it<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">How much data we have<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">How noisy the real world is<br>
</li>
</ul>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Why This Matters in Machine Learning</strong>
</h3>
Understanding the target function concept helps us see the entire ML process clearly:
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Overfitting means:<br>
( h(x) ) matches training data too closely, but not ( f(x) )<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Underfitting means:<br>
( h(x) ) is too simple to match ( f(x) )<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Good generalization means:<br>
( h(x) <span class="math math-inline is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML"><mjx-math class="MJX-TEX"><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2248"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-math></mjx-container></span>  f(x) ) on unseen data<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The moment we accept that (f(x)) is hidden and only approximable, machine learning stops being a guessing game and becomes a controlled, principled process.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Numerical Example (Simple Illustration)</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Suppose the true relationship between study hours and exam score is:</p>
<div class="math math-block is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML" display="true"><mjx-math display="true" class="MJX-TEX" style="margin-left: 0px; margin-right: 0px;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D453 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c3D"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mn class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c31"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c30"></mjx-c></mjx-mn><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="3"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2B"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mn class="mjx-n" space="3"><mjx-c class="mjx-c32"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c30"></mjx-c></mjx-mn></mjx-math></mjx-container></div>
<p dir="auto">But we <strong>don’t know</strong> this function.</p>
<p dir="auto">We only observe 3 sample points:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">(1 hour, 35 marks)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">(2 hours, 40 marks)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">(3 hours, 48 marks)<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Due to noise, the observed outputs do not match the perfect line (10x + 20).</p>
<p dir="auto">Now suppose we choose a linear model:</p>
<div class="math math-block is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML" display="true"><mjx-math display="true" class="MJX-TEX" style="margin-left: 0px; margin-right: 0px;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c210E TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c3D"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-msub space="4"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D703 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: -0.15em;"><mjx-mn class="mjx-n" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c30"></mjx-c></mjx-mn></mjx-script></mjx-msub><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="3"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2B"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-msub space="3"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D703 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: -0.15em;"><mjx-mn class="mjx-n" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c31"></mjx-c></mjx-mn></mjx-script></mjx-msub><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi></mjx-math></mjx-container></div>
<p dir="auto">We fit it to the observed data and get:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><span class="math math-inline is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML"><mjx-math class="MJX-TEX"><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-msub><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D703 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: -0.15em;"><mjx-mn class="mjx-n" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c30"></mjx-c></mjx-mn></mjx-script></mjx-msub><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c3D"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mn class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c32"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c32"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c2E"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c30"></mjx-c></mjx-mn><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-math></mjx-container></span><br>
</li>
<li dir="auto"><span class="math math-inline is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML"><mjx-math class="MJX-TEX"><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-msub><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D703 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: -0.15em;"><mjx-mn class="mjx-n" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c31"></mjx-c></mjx-mn></mjx-script></mjx-msub><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c3D"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mn class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c38"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c2E"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c35"></mjx-c></mjx-mn><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-math></mjx-container></span><br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">So:</p>
<div class="math math-block is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML" display="true"><mjx-math display="true" class="MJX-TEX" style="margin-left: 0px; margin-right: 0px;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c210E TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c3D"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mn class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c32"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c32"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c2E"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c30"></mjx-c></mjx-mn><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="3"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2B"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mn class="mjx-n" space="3"><mjx-c class="mjx-c38"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c2E"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c35"></mjx-c></mjx-mn><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi></mjx-math></mjx-container></div>
<p dir="auto">This is clearly <strong>not the true function</strong>, but:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">It captures the upward trend<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">It generalizes reasonably<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">It approximates (f(x)) as well as possible given limited data<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Thus:</p>
<div class="math math-block is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML" display="true"><mjx-math display="true" class="MJX-TEX" style="margin-left: 0px; margin-right: 0px;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c210E TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2248"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D453 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-math></mjx-container></div>
<p dir="auto">This is the essence of machine learning.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Final Summary</strong>
</h3>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">The target function (f(x)) represents the true relationship in the world.<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">We never see (f(x)) directly — only input–output examples.<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Learning is the process of constructing a hypothesis (h(x)) that approximates (f(x)).<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">The chosen hypothesis space limits what kinds of functions (h(x)) can represent.<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Understanding (f(x)) vs (h(x)) is essential to reasoning about underfitting, overfitting, generalization, and model selection.<br>
</li>
</ul>
<hr>
<hr>
<h2 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Choosing a Learning Algorithm</strong>
</h2>
<p dir="auto">Choosing a learning algorithm is like choosing <em>how</em> to search for treasure in a vast landscape.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">The <strong>hypothesis space</strong> tells us <em>where</em> the treasure might be.<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">The <strong>learning algorithm</strong> tells us <em>how</em> we search for it.<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Different learning algorithms use different strategies, assumptions, and tools for navigating the hypothesis space. Some crawl slowly but safely, some jump around cleverly, and some follow gradients like mountain climbers.</p>
<p dir="auto">Let us explore what “choosing a learning algorithm” truly means.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">The Learning Algorithm Is a Search Strategy</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Once we define a hypothesis space — say, all linear functions, or all neural networks with 3 layers — we still need a way to find the <strong>best</strong> hypothesis inside it.</p>
<p dir="auto">The core idea:</p>
<blockquote dir="auto">
<p><strong>Learning is a search for the hypothesis that best fits the data.</strong></p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Let the set of all possible hypotheses be:</p>
<div class="math math-block is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML" display="true"><mjx-math display="true" class="MJX-TEX" style="margin-left: 0px; margin-right: 0px;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D43B TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c3D"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-texatom space="4" texclass="ORD"><mjx-msub><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c210E TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: -0.15em;"><mjx-mn class="mjx-n" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c31"></mjx-c></mjx-mn></mjx-script></mjx-msub><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2C"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-msub space="2"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c210E TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: -0.15em;"><mjx-mn class="mjx-n" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c32"></mjx-c></mjx-mn></mjx-script></mjx-msub><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2C"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-msub space="2"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c210E TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: -0.15em;"><mjx-mn class="mjx-n" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c33"></mjx-c></mjx-mn></mjx-script></mjx-msub><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2C"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="2"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2026"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-texatom></mjx-math></mjx-container></div>
<p dir="auto">We want to find:</p>
<div class="math math-block is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML" display="true"><mjx-math display="true" class="MJX-TEX" style="margin-left: 0px; margin-right: 0px;"><mjx-msup><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c210E TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: 0.413em;"><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2217"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-script></mjx-msup><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c3D"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c61"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c72"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c67"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2061"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-munder space="2"><mjx-row><mjx-base><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c6D"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c69"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c6E"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-base></mjx-row><mjx-row><mjx-under style="padding-top: 0.167em; padding-left: 0.08em;"><mjx-texatom size="s" texclass="ORD"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c210E TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2208"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D43B TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi></mjx-texatom></mjx-under></mjx-row></mjx-munder><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c3B"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" space="2"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D452 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D45F TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D45F TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D45C TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D45F TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c210E TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-math></mjx-container></div>
<p dir="auto">But simply enumerating all hypotheses is impossible — hypothesis spaces are often infinite.</p>
<p dir="auto">So we need <strong>algorithms</strong>.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Why Different Algorithms Exist</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Different learning algorithms exist because different hypothesis spaces require different search strategies.</p>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Decision trees need ID3 / C4.5</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">These algorithms greedily choose the feature with maximum information gain.</p>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Neural networks need backpropagation</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">A gradient-based method that tunes millions of weights.</p>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">SVMs need quadratic or SMO optimization</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Specialized solvers handle constraints and margins.</p>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">kNN doesn’t “train”</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Its algorithm is a simple lookup structure: “store the data.”</p>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Bayesian models need probability computations</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">They derive hypotheses by maximizing posterior probability.</p>
<p dir="auto">Thus, the choice of algorithm is inseparable from the representation and hypothesis space.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Algorithms Search Using Optimization Principles</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Most modern algorithms are essentially <strong>optimization engines</strong>.</p>
<p dir="auto">They start with some initial guess (e.g., random weights) and iteratively move toward a solution minimizing a loss function:</p>
<div class="math math-block is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML" display="true"><mjx-math display="true" class="MJX-TEX" style="margin-left: 0px; margin-right: 0px;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D43D TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D703 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-math></mjx-container></div>
<p dir="auto">The goal:</p>
<div class="math math-block is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML" display="true"><mjx-math display="true" class="MJX-TEX" style="margin-left: 0px; margin-right: 0px;"><mjx-msup><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D703 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: 0.413em;"><mjx-texatom size="s" texclass="ORD"><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2217"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-texatom></mjx-script></mjx-msup><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c3D"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c61"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c72"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c67"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2061"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-munder space="2"><mjx-row><mjx-base><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c6D"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c69"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c6E"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-base></mjx-row><mjx-row><mjx-under style="padding-top: 0.167em; padding-left: 0.668em;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D703 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi></mjx-under></mjx-row></mjx-munder><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" space="2"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D43D TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D703 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-math></mjx-container></div>
<p dir="auto">This might represent:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Sum of squared errors (linear regression)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Cross-entropy loss (logistic regression, neural nets)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Margin-based loss (SVMs)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Negative log-likelihood (probabilistic models)<br>
</li>
</ul>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Gradient Descent — the Universal Workhorse</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Many algorithms rely on <strong>gradient descent</strong> because it gives a simple recipe:</p>
<blockquote dir="auto">
<p>“Follow the direction of steepest descent on the error surface.”</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">The update rule is:</p>
<div class="math math-block is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML" display="true"><mjx-math display="true" class="MJX-TEX" style="margin-left: 0px; margin-right: 0px;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D703 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c3A"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c3D"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D703 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="3"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2212"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" space="3"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D6FC TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-msub><mjx-mi class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2207"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: -0.15em;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D703 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi></mjx-script></mjx-msub><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D43D TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D703 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-math></mjx-container></div>
<p dir="auto">Where:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><span class="math math-inline is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML"><mjx-math class="MJX-TEX"><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D703 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-math></mjx-container></span> are model parameters<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto"><span class="math math-inline is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML"><mjx-math class="MJX-TEX"><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D6FC TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-math></mjx-container></span> is the learning rate<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto"><span class="math math-inline is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML"><mjx-math class="MJX-TEX"><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-msub><mjx-mi class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2207"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: -0.15em;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D703 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi></mjx-script></mjx-msub><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D43D TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D703 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-math></mjx-container></span> is the gradient<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">This lets the model move through a high-dimensional landscape, step by step, toward a good solution.</p>
<p dir="auto">It works beautifully for:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Linear regression<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Logistic regression<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Neural networks<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Many deep learning models<br>
</li>
</ul>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Greedy Algorithms — fast but approximate</strong>
</h3>
Some hypothesis spaces cannot support smooth gradient surfaces.
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Decision Trees:</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Algorithms like <strong>ID3</strong> and <strong>C4.5</strong> make greedy, local decisions:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Pick the feature that splits the data best<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Repeat recursively<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Stop when purity is high<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">These algorithms don’t guarantee the <em>global</em> best tree — but they produce good trees quickly.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Probabilistic Algorithms — reasoning under uncertainty</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Some algorithms choose the best hypothesis by calculating <strong>probabilities</strong>.</p>
<p dir="auto">Examples:</p>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Naive Bayes</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Find hypothesis <span class="math math-inline is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML"><mjx-math class="MJX-TEX"><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c210E TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2208"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D43B TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-math></mjx-container></span> that maximizes:</p>
<div class="math math-block is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML" display="true"><mjx-math display="true" class="MJX-TEX" style="margin-left: 0px; margin-right: 0px;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D443 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c210E TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2223"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D437 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D44E TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D461 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D44E TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-math></mjx-container></div>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Bayesian Networks</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Use structured probability models.</p>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Expectation–Maximization (EM)</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Refines hidden variable models by alternating between:</p>
<ol>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Expectation step</strong>: infer hidden data</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Maximization step</strong>: update parameters</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">Probabilistic algorithms are crucial when uncertainty matters deeply.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Instance-Based Algorithms — no training at all</strong>
</h3>
Algorithms like kNN flip the idea of learning:
<ul>
<li dir="auto">No weights<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">No fitting<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">No optimization<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">They simply <strong>store</strong> all training examples.</p>
<p dir="auto">During prediction:</p>
<blockquote dir="auto">
<p>Find the nearest stored instances → make a decision.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Learning happens “on demand” during prediction.</p>
<p dir="auto">This simplicity makes kNN powerful for data with strong <em>local</em> structure.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Algorithm Choice Depends on the Nature of the Problem</strong>
</h3>
Different real-world problems demand different algorithmic behaviors.
<p dir="auto">Let’s examine how various aspects influence the choice.</p>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Data Size</strong>
</h4>
<ul>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Huge datasets</strong> → linear models, SGD, shallow neural nets<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto"><strong>Small datasets</strong> → decision trees, SVMs, probabilistic models<br>
</li>
</ul>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Dimensionality</strong>
</h4>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">High-dimensional data (text, images) → SVM with linear kernel, deep networks<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Low-dimensional data → kNN, decision trees<br>
</li>
</ul>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Interpretability Needs</strong>
</h4>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Doctors need explanations → Logistic regression, decision trees<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">No need for interpretability → Deep nets, boosted trees<br>
</li>
</ul>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Noise Tolerance</strong>
</h4>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Noisy data → Regularized linear models, SVMs<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Low noise → Decision trees, nearest-neighbor<br>
</li>
</ul>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Computational Constraints</strong>
</h4>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Neural networks require GPUs<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">SVMs may be slow for large datasets<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Linear models are extremely fast<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Thus, choosing the algorithm is a careful engineering decision.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Numerical Example — Choosing a Learning Algorithm</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">A bank wants to predict loan defaulters using:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Income<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Credit history<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Debt-to-income ratio<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Age<br>
</li>
</ul>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Option A: Decision Tree</strong>
</h4>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Pros: easy to interpret<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Cons: may overfit small datasets<br>
</li>
</ul>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Option B: Logistic Regression</strong>
</h4>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Pros: fast, interpretable<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Cons: limited to linear boundaries<br>
</li>
</ul>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Option C: SVM with RBF Kernel</strong>
</h4>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Pros: strong performance<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Cons: slow on large datasets<br>
</li>
</ul>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Option D: Neural Network</strong>
</h4>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Pros: handles nonlinear interactions<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Cons: needs much data, tuning, compute<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Assume the dataset has:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">5,000 examples<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Moderate noise<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Requirement: explainability for regulation<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Best Choice: Logistic Regression or a small Decision Tree<br>
because they offer a balance between accuracy and interpretability.</p>
<p dir="auto">This illustrates how algorithm choice depends on practical constraints.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Final Summary</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Choosing the learning algorithm is choosing how the system will search the hypothesis space.<br>
It determines:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">How the model learns<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">How fast it learns<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">How much data it needs<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">How complex a function it can represent<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">How well it generalizes<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Every algorithm carries unique assumptions, strengths, and weaknesses.</p>
<p dir="auto">A good ML designer understands the landscape and chooses the algorithm whose search strategy matches the structure of the problem.</p>
<hr>
<hr>
<h2 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Choosing a Representation for Input</strong>
</h2>
<p dir="auto">When we look at a dataset, we often focus on the algorithm:<br>
“Should I use logistic regression? SVM? Neural networks?”</p>
<p dir="auto">But before any algorithm even begins learning, something far more fundamental decides whether learning is even possible.</p>
<p dir="auto">That fundamental element is representation.</p>
<p dir="auto">Representation is the language in which the data speaks to the algorithm.</p>
<p dir="auto">If the language is poor, distorted, or incomplete, even the most powerful algorithm becomes helpless.<br>
If the language is rich, precise, and meaningful, even a simple algorithm becomes surprisingly effective.</p>
<p dir="auto">Let’s unfold why.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">The Algorithm Sees the World Only Through Representation</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Consider an image of a handwritten digit “5”.</p>
<p dir="auto">Your eyes perceive:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Curves<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Shape<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Thickness<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Orientation<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">But to a machine learning algorithm, the same “5” may be represented as:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">784 grayscale pixel intensities (MNIST)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">A vector of edge orientations<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">A compressed embedding from a convolutional neural network<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Each representation tells a different story about the same image.</p>
<p dir="auto">Thus:</p>
<blockquote dir="auto">
<p>Representation determines what the model can see.<br>
What it cannot see, it cannot learn.</p>
</blockquote>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Features Are the “Inputs” to the Learning Algorithm</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Every input is converted into measurable properties called features.</p>
<p dir="auto">These features might be:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Numeric (age, income, height)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Categorical (color = red/blue/green)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Binary (spam/not spam)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Structured (trees, graphs)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Sequences (sentences)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Images (pixels)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Audio (waveforms, MFCCs)<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The learner receives only these features.</p>
<p dir="auto">So the question becomes:</p>
<blockquote dir="auto">
<p>Which features best capture the essence of the problem?</p>
</blockquote>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Good Representations Make Learning Easy</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">A good representation:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Simplifies the underlying pattern<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Makes the target function less complicated<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Makes the hypothesis space effective<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Reduces the burden on the learning algorithm<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Consider the classic example from Tom Mitchell:</p>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Learning to recognize days with high sales</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Poor representation:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">“Is it a holiday? yes/no”<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">“Number of customers”<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Good representation:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Trend information (moving averages)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Day-of-week patterns<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Special event encoding<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Weather encoding<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Better features → clearer patterns → easier learning.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Bad Representations Make Learning Impossible</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Examples:</p>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Failure Case 1 — Wrong Encoding</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Representing a nominal feature (e.g., “color”) as:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">red → 1<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">blue → 2<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">green → 3<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">This accidentally tells the model that “green &gt; blue &gt; red,”<br>
which is meaningless.</p>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Failure Case 2 — Missing Key Information</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Trying to predict house prices but missing:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Location<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Size<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Number of bedrooms<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">The model becomes blind.</p>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Failure Case 3 — Redundant and Noisy Features</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Many irrelevant columns → higher dimensionality → curse of dimensionality.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Choosing a Representation is Choosing a Worldview</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Different algorithms expect different kinds of input:</p>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Linear Models</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Expect data in a nice tabular form:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Numeric columns<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Clean normalization<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">No weird distributions<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">They assume straight-line separability.</p>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Decision Trees</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Are flexible with representation:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Handle categories well<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Don’t need scaling<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Can handle missing values<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">They prefer features that split the data meaningfully.</p>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Neural Networks</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Can digest:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Images<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Sound<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Text<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Sensor data<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">But they often require dense numeric vectors.</p>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">SVMs</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Work best with:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Properly scaled continuous features<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Kernel-transformed inputs<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">They hate:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">High redundancy<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Non-standard scales<br>
</li>
</ul>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">kNN</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Depends heavily on distance representation:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">If distance is meaningful → works well<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">If poorly scaled → fails completely</li>
</ul>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Feature Engineering — Crafting Representation</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Feature engineering is the art of creating better representations.</p>
<p dir="auto">Examples:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Log-transforming skewed features<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Normalizing income or age<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Creating ratios (debt-to-income)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Encoding categories with one-hot vectors<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Extracting edges from images<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Using TF-IDF for text<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">This process determines how easy or hard the learning task becomes.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">The Representation–Hypothesis Interaction</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Representation and hypothesis space always interact.</p>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Example</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">You choose linear regression but your data is nonlinear.</p>
<p dir="auto">Option 1: Change the representation<br>
Introduce polynomial features:</p>
<div class="math math-block is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML" display="true"><mjx-math display="true" class="MJX-TEX" style="margin-left: 0px; margin-right: 0px;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2C"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="2"><mjx-c class="mjx-c3B"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-msup space="2"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: 0.413em;"><mjx-mn class="mjx-n" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c32"></mjx-c></mjx-mn></mjx-script></mjx-msup><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2C"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="2"><mjx-c class="mjx-c3B"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-msup space="2"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D465 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-script style="vertical-align: 0.413em;"><mjx-mn class="mjx-n" size="s"><mjx-c class="mjx-c33"></mjx-c></mjx-mn></mjx-script></mjx-msup></mjx-math></mjx-container></div>
<p dir="auto">Option 2: Change the algorithm<br>
Use a neural network or SVM with RBF kernel.</p>
<p dir="auto">Thus:</p>
<blockquote dir="auto">
<p>Choosing representation sometimes transforms the learning problem into a simpler one.</p>
</blockquote>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Representation Determines the Shape of the Target Function</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Even if the true function (f(x)) is nonlinear,<br>
a good representation can make it look linear.</p>
<p dir="auto">Example:</p>
<p dir="auto">To predict area of a square:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">True relationship:<br>
( \text{Area} = s^2 )<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Representation 1: use feature “s” → nonlinear, needs complex model<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Representation 2: use feature “s²” → perfectly linear<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Thus representation can simplify the world.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Numerical Example — Good vs Bad Representation</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Suppose we want to predict whether a student will pass or fail.</p>
<p dir="auto">Data available:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Study hours<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Mood<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Sleep hours<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Mobile usage<br>
</li>
</ul>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Case 1 — Bad Representation</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Use only:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Mood (“happy/sad” encoded as 1/2)<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Mobile usage in minutes<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Missing study hours makes prediction almost meaningless.</p>
<p dir="auto">The model might attempt to learn random correlations.</p>
<hr>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Case 2 — Good Representation</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Use:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Study hours<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Slee</li>
</ul>
<hr>
<hr>
<h2 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Perspectives in Machine Learning</strong>
</h2>
<p dir="auto">Different viewpoints exist on what “learning” really means.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Learning as Function Approximation</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">This viewpoint says:</p>
<blockquote dir="auto">
<p>“The learner finds a function that best maps inputs to outputs.”</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Regression, neural networks, SVMs — all follow this idea.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Learning as Probability Estimation</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Here, the goal is to model uncertainty:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">What is the probability this email is spam?<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">What is the probability of disease?<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">This is central to Bayesian learning and logistic regression.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Learning as Optimization</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Another perspective sees learning as:</p>
<blockquote dir="auto">
<p>“Find the parameters that minimize error.”</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Many algorithms boil down to:</p>
<div class="math math-block is-loaded"><mjx-container class="MathJax" jax="CHTML" display="true"><mjx-math display="true" class="MJX-TEX" style="margin-left: 0px; margin-right: 0px;"><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D703 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c3A"></mjx-c><mjx-c class="mjx-c3D"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" space="4"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D703 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n" space="3"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2212"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i" space="3"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D6FC TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mi class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c2207"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D43D TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c28"></mjx-c></mjx-mo><mjx-mi class="mjx-i"><mjx-c class="mjx-c1D703 TEX-I"></mjx-c></mjx-mi><mjx-mo class="mjx-n"><mjx-c class="mjx-c29"></mjx-c></mjx-mo></mjx-math></mjx-container></div>
<p dir="auto">Learning is climbing/descending a landscape.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Learning as Pattern Recognition</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Humans are good at noticing patterns.<br>
Machine learning formalizes this:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Detect clusters<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Separate classes<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Find structure in data<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Pattern recognition is especially central for kNN, SVMs, neural networks.</p>
<hr>
<hr>
<h2 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Issues in Machine Learning</strong>
</h2>
<p dir="auto">Machine learning is powerful, but fragile. Several fundamental issues shape its success.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">The Problem of Overfitting</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">A model may fit the noise instead of the true pattern.</p>
<p dir="auto">Symptoms:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Perfect training accuracy<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Terrible test accuracy<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Overfitting is the central danger in ML.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">The Bias–Variance Dilemma</strong>
</h3>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">High bias → model too simple<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">High variance → model too complex<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Balancing these is key to good generalization.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">The Curse of Dimensionality</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">As features increase:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Distances become meaningless<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Data becomes sparse<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Overfitting skyrockets<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">kNN and RBF are especially sensitive.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Noise and Insufficient Data</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Learning is only as good as the data.</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Incorrect labels<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Missing values<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Small datasets<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Hidden variables<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">These create fundamental limits.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Computational Constraints</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">Large hypothesis spaces require:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Efficient algorithms<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Good optimization<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Smart data structures<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">This is why algorithms like SMO for SVMs are critical.</p>
<hr>
<h3 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Evaluation and Generalization</strong>
</h3>
<p dir="auto">We must test hypotheses on data not seen before.<br>
This leads to:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Validation sets<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Test sets<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Cross-validation<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Confidence intervals<br>
</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">Generalization is the final goal of ML.</p>
<hr>
<hr>
<h2 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Numerical Example – Well-Posed Learning Problem</strong>
</h2>
<p dir="auto">Let’s define a learning scenario.</p>
<p dir="auto">A supermarket wants a system to predict whether a customer will buy a product (yes/no) based on:</p>
<ul>
<li dir="auto">Age<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Income<br>
</li>
<li dir="auto">Shopping history<br>
</li>
</ul>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Step 1: Define Task (T)</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Binary classification:<br>
“Predict purchase decision.”</p>
<h4 style="text-align: left; color: blue;" class="page-header" dir="auto">
  <strong style="color: #cc33cc;">Step 2: Define Performance (P)</strong>
</h4>
<p dir="auto">Use accuracy:</p>
